Third, funding comes from a single source. Buying and repairing tools currently depends entirely on subdistrict funding; should that funding shrink, the project would be hard to sustain.

4. Analysis of causes
The problems above have both objective and institutional-design causes. Objectively, the tool rooms were converted from vacant rooms in the communities; they are small and poorly equipped, and full-time managers cannot yet be provided, so they rely on volunteers taking turns, which naturally limits opening hours. In terms of design, the project was launched rather hastily, and issues such as borrowing rules and compensation standards were not thought through. Publicity also needs strengthening. Among respondents who have never borrowed, over 40% said they 'didn't know this place existed', which shows the project is still not well known. Some residents know about the rooms but worry that 'if something gets broken, it'll be hard to sort out', and so are reluctant to borrow. This reflects, on the one hand, that the rules are not transparent enough, and on the other, that trust among neighbours has yet to be built.

5. Recommendations
Based on the above analysis, the team makes the following recommendations: first, improve the borrowing rules by introducing a deposit or credit-points system, clarify liability for damage or loss, and reward residents who return items on time; second, extend opening hours, trying weekend and weekday-evening openings, and introduce self-service lockers for borrowing and returning, to make things easier for office workers; third, broaden funding sources: besides government funds, encourage nearby businesses to donate tools or provide repair services, and explore charging a small maintenance fee; fourth, step up publicity through community WeChat groups, notice boards and other channels to raise residents' awareness of the service.

6. Conclusion
Overall, the 'tool-sharing room' is a low-cost, high-benefit model of community service. Its significance lies not only in letting residents 'spend less and get more done', but also in offering increasingly distant urban neighbours a chance to reconnect. Although the project still has problems such as non-standard management and limited reach, as long as improvements are made in the areas above, this kind of model is fully capable of being extended on a larger scale. The team suggests that the relevant departments, building on the experience of the three pilot communities, expand the pilot to more communities next year and re-evaluate its effects a year later.
